content: Adalimumab is a medication that works by inhibiting a protein called tumor necrosis factor (TNF), which is part of the immune system. TNF is known to contribute to joint swelling and damage in arthritis, as well as red, scaly patches in psoriasis. Adalimumab belongs to a class of drugs known as TNF blockers. Before starting adalimumab, it is essential to read the Medication Guide and Instructions for Use provided by your pharmacist. These should also be reviewed each time you receive a refill. Consult your healthcare provider for guidance on how to properly prepare and administer this medication. Adalimumab is administered via subcutaneous injection, typically in the thigh or abdomen, as directed by your doctor. The frequency of administration is usually every other week, but in some cases, it may be given once a week. The dosage is determined based on your medical condition and response to treatment. For children, the dosage is also calculated based on weight. If you are using adalimumab to treat conditions such as psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or uveitis, your doctor may prescribe a different dosing schedule or a higher initial dose. Before injecting, remove the medication from the refrigerator and allow it to reach room temperature for 15 to 30 minutes. Do not warm the medication using other methods, such as microwaving or placing it in hot water. Inspect the liquid for particles or discoloration before use; if either is present, do not use the medication. Clean the injection site with rubbing alcohol before administering the dose. Rotate injection sites to minimize skin injury, ensuring each new site is at least 5 centimeters away from the previous one. Avoid injecting into skin that is sore, bruised, red, or hard. To reduce bruising, do not rub the injection site after administering the medication. Use adalimumab regularly to achieve the maximum benefit. Mark your calendar to help you remember your scheduled doses. Common side effects may include redness, itching, pain, or swelling at the injection site. However, your doctor has prescribed this medication because they believe the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Adalimumab may rarely cause severe, potentially fatal liver disease in individuals exposed to the hepatitis B virus. Your doctor may order blood tests and monitor for symptoms during treatment and for several months after your last dose. Serious allergic reactions to this medication are rare but possible. Adalimumab can increase your susceptibility to infections or worsen existing infections. Avoid contact with individuals who have contagious infections, such as chickenpox, COVID-19, measles, or the flu. Inform your healthcare provider that you are using adalimumab before receiving any vaccinations. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly necessary, as it may harm an unborn baby. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Adalimumab can also pass into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal supplements, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. In the event of an overdose, if someone exhibits severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. While using this medication, regular lab tests, such as complete blood counts and liver function tests, may be required. Keep all medical and lab appointments as scheduled. If you miss a dose, consult your doctor or pharmacist promptly for a new dosing schedule. Store adalimumab in the refrigerator and do not freeze it. Keep the medication in its original container to protect it from light. Some brands may also be stored at room temperature if necessary; consult your pharmacist or the product packaging for specific storage instructions. Discard any unused portion of the medication properly. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. This medication can suppress your immune system, reducing your ability to fight infections. This effect may lead to serious, potentially fatal infections, including fungal or bacterial infections such as tuberculosis. Inform your doctor of your medical history, particularly any past or current infections. Additionally, let your doctor know if you have lived or traveled in areas where certain fungal infections, such as coccidioidomycosis or histoplasmosis, are common, or if you have been in contact with someone with tuberculosis. These infections are more prevalent in regions such as the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and the southwestern United States. Your doctor will test you for tuberculosis before and during treatment with this medication. Although rare, there is a potential risk of developing cancer, such as lymphoma or skin cancer, particularly in children, teens, and young adults. Discuss the risks and benefits of treatment with your doctor. This information is not exhaustive and does not replace professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
